narrative:
The model estimated a 51.0% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is just above an even chance, but it was treated as sufficient reason to deny your law school application. The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class standing: at 1.00, it was far below the average of about 5.79 among accepted students, and it was the single strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your first-year standing, also 1.00 compared with an accepted-student average near 6.00, was the third most influential factor and likewise pushed toward failure. Between those two, your low family-income bracket was the second most important factor, but it pushed in the opposite direction—toward passing. This is notable because low-income students are only a small share of accepted students, about 2.2%, yet the model did not treat your income as a reason to deny you. Still, the two weak class-standing indicators outweighed that countervailing signal, leaving the predicted failure risk just over half.

Next, ask for a human review of the denial rather than accepting the model output as final. Explain any circumstances behind your first- and third-year rankings, provide evidence of improvement or grade context, and ask what academic-support or bar-preparation steps would strengthen a future application. If possible, address your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA through retaking or additional coursework, and request that the admissions committee consider your full record, not just the model's 51.0% estimate.
